1422.title: The chief end (Westminster Shorter Catechism, 1647)
1422.hook: Q1: our chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever
1422.howItsDone: In Presbyterian and other Reformed churches, children and new members can learn the Westminster Shorter Catechism by question and answer, starting from this first question.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mystery of love: love doesn't explain suffering, but walks into it. Your line was love enters.

A question, written for teaching: "What is the chief end of man?" Chief end. The main thing a human life is for. You might expect a long answer: duty, rules, a list of obligations. The answer is one sentence: "Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever." It opens the Westminster Shorter Catechism, a little book of questions that Presbyterian and other Reformed churches use to teach the faith. This path met that sentence once before, in passing. Today it gets a whole day.
screen: `WHAT IS THE CHIEF END OF MAN?`

segments.voice: Start with the word end. Here it doesn't mean the finish line. It means purpose, the thing something is for, the way a key is for opening a door. So the question is: what is a person for? Now look at the grammar. Glorify, and enjoy: two verbs, but one end, singular. The catechism doesn't give a life a serious purpose and, separately, a pleasant one. It joins them with a single and: giving God glory and delighting in God are one thing. Then two words at the close: for ever. Not only on good days. That's where the sentence meets these last weeks of hard questions. The catechism backs its answers with scripture, and one passage given here is Psalm seventy-three. After one line on God's goodness, it turns to a man who nearly gave up: "my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped." He watched cruel people do well and good people suffer, and it was "too painful for me." Until he went into the sanctuary of God. Then: "Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee." And, still honest: "My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever." His body failing, his heart failing, and still, enjoyment of God. Paul brings the same end down to the kitchen table: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." A whole teaching about God, and its first answer has the word enjoy in it.
screen: `EAT, OR DRINK: TO THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing within reach, the warmth of a cup, light on a wall, the taste of what you last ate, a sound from the next room, and stay with it, without analyzing, until it is simply good to you. If you pray, let that enjoyment be your thanks, without adding words; if you don't, let the small thing be enough for now.
The chief end. In the Westminster Shorter Catechism, what a human life is for: to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever. One end, with two verbs.
Your line: glorify and enjoy. Paul put eating and drinking on the list. See you tomorrow.

1423.title: What am I for?
1423.hook: every life is called to love in its own way
1423.howItsDone: Christians talk about calling, or vocation, in many settings: some churches pray for people in their daily work, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of callings to marriage, single life, priesthood and religious life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chief end: to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever. Your line was glorify and enjoy.

Night, in the temple of the LORD at Shiloh. A boy named Samuel is lying down, and the lamp hasn't gone out yet. He hears his name, gets up, and runs to the old priest, Eli: "Here am I; for thou calledst me." Eli says he didn't call. Go back to bed. It happens again. And again. Samuel keeps running to the wrong person. Finally Eli understands, and tells the boy what to say next time. When the voice comes, Samuel answers: "Speak; for thy servant heareth." Yesterday asked what a human life is for. Today asks it smaller, and closer: what is my life for?
screen: `A BOY HEARS HIS NAME AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Paul's Greek word for calling is klesis. He writes to the church in Corinth, people who were slaves and free, married and single: "Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called." Calling, and called, side by side. The ordinary life you're in when the call finds you can be the place where you answer it. Martin Luther and other reformers pressed this hard: a calling isn't only for priests, monks and nuns. A farmer, a parent, a shoemaker can each have one. Catholic teaching speaks of a universal call to holiness, for every baptized person in whatever state of life. Orthodox writers speak of every life as a way toward God. The churches put it differently; the shared thread is that the call isn't kept for a few. So what is everyone called to? Paul tells the Galatians: "ye have been called unto liberty," and then what the freedom is for: "by love serve one another." The shape of the call is love. Your own way of loving is the part that differs: fixing things, listening, teaching, sitting up with a sick parent. And notice Samuel. He heard the call before he knew who was calling, and kept running to the wrong person. Some readers find comfort in that: a calling can take more than one try, and sometimes another person, like old Eli, helps you hear it.

Skip the job titles, and think of the people in your life and the way you most often end up loving them: fixing, feeding, listening, making them laugh, telling the truth. Let one line come that starts, I am called to love by, and finish it yourself; if it doesn't come yet, that's all right, Samuel needed more than one call. If you pray, you can say Samuel's words, speak; for thy servant heareth, and then wait.
Calling. Klesis, Paul's word for it. In his letters, a call that finds people in ordinary lives, and whose shape is love.
Your line: called to love. Each life in its own way. I'll be here tomorrow.

1424.title: Faith as trust
1424.hook: the Greek word pistis means trust, faithfulness, loyalty
1424.howItsDone: Christians speak of faith as trusting God in daily life, and some bring their worries to God in prayer, alone or by asking others in their church to pray with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, calling: a boy who heard his name at night and kept running to the wrong person. Your line was called to love.

"Master, master, we perish." A small boat filling with water, a storm of wind come down on the lake, and men shouting. Jesus is asleep in the boat. They wake him. He rebukes the wind and the waves, and there is a calm. Then he turns to his friends with one short question: "Where is your faith?" He doesn't ask what they believe about him. They'd just called him master. He asks where their faith went when the water came in.

The New Testament's word for faith is pistis, and in Greek it's a wide word: trust, faithfulness, and loyalty, the kind you keep to a friend. So when the Gospels talk about faith, they don't only mean holding a list of ideas to be true. They mean leaning your weight on someone. That's why the question in the boat lands so hard. The disciples ran to him for help; what they couldn't do, with the boat filling, was trust him. Luke even says that afterward they asked one another what manner of man this was. They were still working out who he was. The Letter to the Hebrews pictures faith as nearly all trust. Abraham is called, and "he went out, not knowing whither he went." No map, just a voice. Proverbs puts it plainly: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding." Churches describe faith in different ways. Martin Luther stressed faith as trust in God's promise. Catholic teaching speaks of a personal clinging to God, and also the mind's assent to what God has revealed. Orthodox writers describe a living relationship. Each holds trust in it somewhere. And trust can live beside doubt. In Mark's Gospel a father with a sick son says in one breath: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." And Jesus heals his son. Trust doesn't mean the storm is gone. It means you're still in the boat, with your weight on someone.

Notice where you're holding your own weight, your shoulders, your jaw, your hands, and let the chair or the floor take it; that's a small trust already. Then bring to mind one person you could lean on a little more: someone to ask for help, to tell something true, or to hand a job you've been gripping. If you pray, you can rest on the proverb's line, trust in the LORD with all thine heart; if you don't, just let the floor hold you.
Faith as trust. Pistis: not only believing something is true, but leaning your weight on someone, even in a storm, even with doubt beside it.
Your line: faith is trust. Even with doubt sitting right beside it. Go gently.

1425.title: Faith as faithfulness
1425.hook: faith is also showing up, again and again
1425.tomorrow: Year four close: the many rooms
1425.howItsDone: Some Christians practice faithfulness through regular habits: daily prayer at set times, weekly worship, and keeping promises such as marriage vows and baptismal vows, including through seasons when faith feels dry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith as trust: a storm, a sleeping teacher, and the question, where is your faith? Your line was faith is trust.

An open window, facing Jerusalem. A new law has just been signed: for thirty days, anyone who prays to any god or man except the king goes to the lions. Daniel knows it's signed. He goes home, up to his room, where the windows are open toward Jerusalem. And the Book of Daniel says he "kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." As he did aforetime. No speech, no protest. He just keeps doing what he did before, at the window, in plain sight.
screen: `A LAW SIGNED: PRAY TO NO ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's Greek word, pistis, meant trust. It also means faithfulness: keeping faith, the way you keep a promise or keep showing up for a friend. When Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit, the King James Bible reads: "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith." Faith, on a list of ways a person acts, right beside gentleness and goodness. Here it reads like faithfulness: something you keep doing. Trust is leaning your weight on someone. Faithfulness is coming back, again and again, whether or not you feel it that day. And one old song puts God's faithfulness before ours. Lamentations is a book of grief, sung over a city in ruins. This path heard the line a few weeks ago; this time, listen for its last word: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Faithfulness, in that line, isn't a feeling. It's what shows up the next day, and the next. The second letter to Timothy has a line for days when faith gives out: "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself." After these weeks of grief and doubt, that line has a job. On a day when you can't feel trust at all, you can still be faithful. You can come back to the window. Daniel's prayer wasn't proof that he felt brave. It was what he did aforetime, done once more.

Bring to mind one thing you used to do faithfully and have let slip, a call, a walk, a prayer, a page of reading, a promise to yourself, and look at it without scolding, the way Daniel looked at his open window. Choose one small way back, smaller than you think it needs to be. If you pray, you can say, great is thy faithfulness; if you don't, simply notice that you showed up here, today.
Faith as faithfulness. Pistis as keeping faith: coming back again and again, like Daniel at his window, held up by a faithfulness that is new every morning.
Your line: keep showing up. Not perfectly, just as you did aforetime. That's today, done.

1426.title: Year four close: the many rooms
1426.hook: thinkers, prayers, ethics, hope and the hardest questions: one house with many rooms (John 14:2)
1426.tomorrow: Four women in the family tree (Matthew 1:1–17)
1426.howItsDone: John 14 is read at some Christian funerals, and some churches return to these chapters of Jesus' last night during Holy Week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith as faithfulness: Daniel at his open window, praying as he did aforetime. Your line was keep showing up.

At the table on Jesus' last night, one of his friends admits he's lost. Jesus has just told them not to be troubled, and that he is going to prepare a place for them. Thomas doesn't nod along: "Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?" This year opened with the promise Thomas was answering, about a house with many rooms. Today the year closes in the same room, with the same line, and Thomas's question still on the table.

John's Gospel, in the King James: "In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you." This year walked that house room by room. The big questions, each church answering in its own voice. Prayer, from the Jesus Prayer to Quaker silence to a hymn. Ethics: commandments, virtues and mercy. The great thinkers, arguing across the centuries. Revelation and Christian hope, from a garden to a garden-city. Church life: rites and spaces, bells and bread. And these last weeks, the hardest room: suffering, doubt, grief, and love that walks into pain without explaining it. Now notice who first heard many mansions. Frightened friends. Peter, just told he would deny Jesus before the rooster crowed. Thomas, saying out loud that he didn't know the way. Right after Peter hears that, Jesus says: "Let not your heart be troubled." And then: "I go to prepare a place for you." A place prepared for them as they are: troubled, unsure, about to fail. Christians read the line in more than one way: some hear it about heaven, some about the church on earth, some about life with God that starts now, and some readers hold those side by side. But in the story, the promise of a room comes before the confusion is cleared up. Thomas asks his question, and what he hears next is an answer, not a rebuke.
screen: `THE YEAR, ONE ROOM AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Walk back through the year's rooms in your mind and notice which one you kept returning to and which one you're standing in today. It might be the room of doubt, with Thomas; that's a room in the house, too. Let one line form, I live in the room of, and finish it yourself; if you pray, offer it to God as it is.
Year four close. The last day of a year spent in one house with many rooms: thinkers, prayer, ethics, hope and the hardest questions. A house first promised to friends who were afraid.
Your line: there is room for you. Tomorrow, year five opens on the first page of Matthew. See you there.
